q: On the old bridge, why were big or frequent calls slow?
options: Every call was turned into text, queued and answered later
JavaScript was not allowed to call native code at all
The phone had no native threads
Native code could only run once at startup
why: The old bridge serialized (turned into text) and queued each call and answered it asynchronously. The cost grew with the size of the data and the number of calls.

q: On the old bridge you could write const value = nativeModule.getValue() and use value on the next line.
why: No. The answer came later, so you passed a callback. With JSI and the New Architecture, a native module can return the value at once.

q: Which of these are part of the New Architecture?
options: JSI, the direct link between JavaScript and C++
TurboModules, native modules loaded when needed
The JSON message queue between JavaScript and native
why: JSI, Fabric, TurboModules and Codegen make the New Architecture. The message queue is the old bridge, and it is gone.

q: Put the versions in order, oldest first.
items: 0.74: Bridgeless is the default with the New Architecture
0.76: the New Architecture is on by default
0.82: the New Architecture is the only option
why: 0.74 in April 2024, 0.76 in October 2024, 0.82 in October 2025. 0.81 and Expo SDK 54 were the last versions that allowed the old architecture.

q: A team turns on the New Architecture and sees no speed up on a heavy screen. What is the best next step?
options: Measure to find the real slow part, because data copying may not be the problem
Switch the old bridge back on
Send bigger objects to native code
why: The docs say enabling it may not immediately improve performance. JSI only helps when copying was the bottleneck. Measure first.

q: Codegen reads a typed description of a module and makes the native ______. (one word: code, interfaces or types)
why: Codegen turns a TypeScript or Flow spec into native interfaces, so a mismatch between JavaScript and native becomes a build error.
